label: in0-engine-power
_why: POWER ON THE ENGINE QUESTION (user-ruled 2026-09-19: 'Do more n on 1836-1838 to better understand the engine situation'). F147 left the engine reading moving two ways at once: adding the supplier point took engine CONSUMPTION from 0.62 to 0.95 of vanilla while the share of engine price readings at the +75% ceiling ROSE from 30% to 45%. Read together that is demand outrunning supply rather than starvation - tight at 0.95 of vanilla's volume instead of tight at 0.62 - but n=2 on a market of ~300 units, supplied by a motor industry of about seven world levels at the 1836 start, cannot separate 'more activity' from 'worse shortage'. This batch takes BOTH arms to n=6 and reads the engine market on its own order book (buy, sell, production) rather than on price alone.

_arms.probe-gradsup: in0-stage 1.40/1.20/1.10 + --in0-supplier 0.5 (map). Four MORE runs; with 20260919_155627's two that is n=6.
_arms.probe-grada: in0-stage 1.40/1.20/1.10, no supplier point. Four MORE runs; with 20260919_142856's two that is n=6. Re-run because the comparison needs power on BOTH sides - the question is a difference between the arms, not a property of one.

_delta: ONE FLAG between the arms: --in0-supplier 0.5. Five industries differ (steel, tooling, paper, fertilizer x1.400 -> x1.300; explosives x1.325 -> x1.225); the other twelve are byte-identical.

_predictions._basis: F147 at n=2 each. Stated before the runs.
_predictions.the_question: Is the engine market's higher ceiling share under gradsup a SUPPLY failure or a DEMAND success? The order book answers it directly. SUPPLY SUCCESS: engine PRODUCTION up against grad-a, motor's staffed levels up, buy/sell ratio roughly unchanged - the market is bigger and just as tight. SUPPLY FAILURE: production flat or down while buy orders rise, buy/sell ratio UP - the extra demand is unmet. Predict the first, because steel is motor's only input and the supplier point made it cheaper: engine production +30-60% against grad-a, motor staffed levels up, buy/sell ratio within 10%.
_predictions.engines_consumed: gradsup 0.95 of vanilla against grad-a's 0.62 at n=2. At n=6 predict the gap holds at 0.25-0.40 and both medians move less than 0.08 from their n=2 values.
_predictions.steel: The n=2 headline was steel's ceiling share 43% -> 15%. Predict it holds within 10 points at n=6; that is the finding F147 rests on and this batch is also its replication.
_predictions.world_product: gradsup 1.00 and grad-a 0.99 of the control at n=2; predict both within 0.02 at n=6, i.e. the one-point gap does NOT survive as a separable claim.
_predictions.null_result: If the two arms' engine order books are indistinguishable at n=6, the F147 engine reading was noise and only the STEEL half of that finding stands.

_reads: early_probe --also across all four probe sessions; the steel and engine market tables; and the engine order book per arm - buy, sell, production and the buy/sell ratio - which is what separates the two hypotheses.
_comparison: The n=2 readings of 20260919_155627 (gradsup) and 20260919_142856 (grad-a), which these runs pool with; vanilla and flat 1.2-1.5 from 20260919_132049.
_watch: run 1 at ~3 min: mod marker, version, this run's error window BY POSITION, clock
engine production and motor staffing in each arm's first summary set
_cost: 8 runs x 1836->1838 ~ 3 min each ~ 28 min including builds and harvest.
_caveats: TWO IN-GAME YEARS IS NOT THE CENTURY.

The engine market is SMALL (~300 units against steel's ~1250) and motor is about seven world levels at 1836, so its readings are intrinsically coarser than steel's; n=6 improves them, it does not make them fine.
Cross-session pooling with two earlier sessions - same machine, day, game version, span and dump dates.
Configs are run back to back, never interleaved (the 2026-09-13 ruling).
Launch ONLY through tools/testbed/launch_detached.ps1 CALLED DIRECTLY from the PowerShell tool (landmine L30); the STOP file must be absent.

defaults._dump_dates_note: Identical to all four earlier probes, which is what makes the sessions poolable.
